name: Hanbang cosmetics

lead: Hanbang is traditional Korean medicine, and hanbang cosmetics apply its herbal ingredients to skincare. Ginseng, green tea and licorice are named examples, and users look to them for brighter, more youthful-looking skin.
A 2025 review of Korean herbs notes antioxidant properties in ingredients like ginseng and green tea and discusses their potential in anti-aging skincare.

paras: Used as creams, essences, masks and similar products formulated with herbal extracts, within a broader K-beauty routine.
Reviews of Korean medicine note that herbs are not automatically safe and that evidence quality varies; skin reactions to any botanical are possible.

angle.text: Hanbang products are used to support a clear, youthful-looking complexion using traditional herbal ingredients.

lead: Hanbang is the Korean tradition of medicine rooted in classical Chinese texts; hanbang cosmetics bring its herbal ingredients into skincare for a healthy, youthful-looking complexion.[1][2]

A 2025 review describes Korean herbal formulations drawing on ginseng, green tea and licorice, whose antioxidant properties are proposed to reduce oxidative stress on skin and slow visible aging.[1] The review also lists herbal masks, teas and acupuncture among related practices.[1]

Korean medicine has deep historical roots: the Donguibogam, written by Heo Jun after the 1592 invasion, integrated Korean and Chinese medicine.[3] Researchers note that Korean medicine trials have often had short observation periods, small samples and subjective outcomes.[4]

paras: Hanbang has origins in classical Chinese texts and is a prominent part of the Korean health care system.[2] The Hyangyak Jipseongbang (1433) promoted domestic ingredients, and Hanbang revived in the late 20th century after decline under Japanese rule.[3]
Reviewers cite ginseng, green tea and licorice as examples with antioxidant activity relevant to skin aging.[1]
K-beauty brands such as Amorepacific popularised natural ingredients globally.[5]

Evidence is mostly laboratory and review literature on bioactive compounds in Korean herbs.[1] A review of health technology assessments of Korean medicines noted small samples and subjective outcomes in trials.[4]
